text: Every gate matrix, Bell state, and teleportation trace in this course so far was computed by exactly the technique this lesson makes explicit: representing a quantum state as an array of numbers and multiplying small matrices into slices of that array. This is literally how a classical computer simulates a quantum circuit — no magic, just arithmetic on an array.

An n-qubit state is stored as a flat array of 2 to the n amplitudes, where each index's binary digits directly encode a basis state — index 6, binary 110, is the amplitude for ket-110. Rather than building a huge, mostly-zero matrix to apply a gate to one qubit, the trick every real simulator uses is to find every pair of indices that differ only in that qubit's bit, and apply the small 2 by 2 gate matrix directly to each pair.

Running this on a 3-qubit system: applying H to qubit 1 of ket-000 gives amplitude 0.7071 at index 0 and index 4 — exactly ket-000 plus ket-100 over root 2. Chaining a CNOT from qubit 1 to qubit 2 onto that moves the index-4 amplitude to index 6, landing on ket-000 plus ket-110 over root 2 — the same Bell state this course derived by hand back in Chapter 3, now reproduced by running real code instead of matrix algebra on paper.

That agreement is the actual test of whether a simulator function is correct: it has to reproduce every result you can already verify independently. This index-pairing approach is exactly what production tools like Qiskit and Q# do under the hood, and it never builds anything larger than the state array itself plus one small, fixed gate matrix.
Next lesson shows exactly where this efficient technique still runs into a hard wall: the state vector itself, not the cost of applying any one gate to it.
